flow.context: This is the first step of the Seen in the Dark test. Here you set up the chair and the dim torch.
flow.do: 1. Find the longest straight path in your home, ending at an open doorway. 2. Put the chair in the doorway, with the next room dark behind it. 3. Hang the black cloth over the chair back. 4. Fold the handkerchief into 4 layers and fix it over the torch with the rubber band.
flow.say: Now you are a driver, and this chair is a person walking on a dark road. The torch is your headlight. We make it dim, because a car's light is weak by the time it reaches someone far away.
flow.kid: Put the chair in a doorway. Keep the room behind it dark. Hang the black cloth on it. Cover the torch with the folded hanky.
flow.parent: The room behind the chair must be dark, with nothing pale behind the cloth, like a real road at night. If the wall behind is white, the black cloth shows up as a dark patch against it, and the test fails. If your home has no free doorway, hang a dark bedsheet behind the chair.

flow.do: 1. Show your child all the cloths in the light. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Your child writes a guess in foot-steps for each cloth in the table.
flow.say: Which cloth do you think you will still see from furthest away? Which will vanish first? Why do you think so? Write a guess for each one.
flow.kid: Look at all the cloths. Write a guess in foot-steps for each one.

ask.q: Why do you think that cloth will be seen from furthest away?
good: It is bright.
White is easy to see.
Black looks like the dark.

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Any guess with a reason is good. A foot-step is one shoe-length: put the heel of one foot against the toes of the other.

flow.do: 1. Switch off all the lights and close the curtains. 2. Wait 2 minutes so your eyes get used to the dark. 3. Your child stands 2 foot-steps from the chair, holding the dim torch against their cheek, pointing at the cloth.
flow.say: Let's wait two minutes in the dark. Your eyes need time to get used to it. Hold the torch right by your eye, like a headlight next to a driver.
flow.kid: Switch off the lights. Wait two minutes for your eyes. Hold the torch by your cheek. Point it at the cloth.
flow.parent: Phone screens and room lights must stay off, so every try has the same darkness.

flow.do: 1. Your child steps backwards, heel to toe, counting foot-steps, keeping the torch on the cloth. 2. They stop when they can no longer tell the cloth is there. 3. Write the number. 4. Switch on the light, change the cloth, switch off, and wait 1 minute. 5. Test every cloth this way.
flow.say: Step back slowly, heel to toe, and count. Keep the torch on the chair. Stop when you can't tell the cloth is there. How many foot-steps?
flow.kid: Step back, heel to toe. Count each step. Keep the torch on the cloth. Stop when it vanishes. Say the number.

ask.q: Which cloth vanished first? How far away were you?
good: The black one, after only a few steps.
The dark one went quickly.

flow.parent: Walk beside your child and keep one hand ready. If even the black cloth is still easy to see at the far end, add 2 more layers of hanky and start again. In many homes the black cloth vanishes within 2 to 5 foot-steps, and the white one may stay visible right to the far wall. If so, write 'still seen at' and the number.

flow.do: 1. Test each cloth a second time, in the same way. 2. Write the second numbers in the table.
flow.say: Scientists try each thing twice, because one try can be a fluke. Let's do every cloth again.
flow.kid: Test each cloth again. Write the new numbers. Are they close to the first ones?

flow.do: 1. If you have a reflective strip or a cycle reflector, put it on the chair. 2. Hold the dim torch next to your eye and shine it at the strip. 3. Then hold the torch at arm's length to the side and look again. 4. Try a piece of kitchen foil the same way.
flow.say: Here is a reflective strip. Hold the torch next to your eye and shine it at the strip. Now hold the torch far out to one side. Does the strip look the same?
flow.kid: Hold the torch by your eye and shine it at the strip. Now hold the torch far to the side. What changed?
flow.parent: The strip blazes when the torch is by the eye, and looks much duller when the torch is held to the side. It sends light back towards the lamp. Foil can glint brightly or look dark, depending on how it is tilted. Skip this step if you have no strip or reflector.

flow.do: 1. Switch the lights on. 2. Read the table together. 3. Ask your child what they found, what shows it, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: What did you find? Which cloth could a driver see from furthest away? What is your evidence? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Look at the table. Which cloth did you see from furthest away? Which vanished first?

ask.q: The same torch shone on every cloth. Why did some vanish sooner?
good: The black cloth sends back very little light.
The white cloth sends back more light to my eyes.

ask.q: What should you wear when you walk on a road at night?
good: White or pale clothes.
Something with a reflective strip.
Carry a torch.

check.q: A girl walks home at night in a black dress. Which change helps drivers see her from furthest away?
options: A white dupatta and a reflective strip on her bag
check.why: A driver sees the girl only by the headlight that bounces off her. A white dupatta reflects much more light than black, and a reflective strip sends the light straight back to the driver. Walking faster does not help the driver see her.

flow.think: You could see the torch's light the whole time. Why could you not see the black cloth?

experiments.title: Words Only: can you send a picture by talking?
experiments.context: In this experiment one person describes a simple picture and the other draws it without seeing it. You find out whether the drawing comes out better when the listener may ask questions.
experiments.question: Does a picture sent by words alone come out more correctly when the listener can ask questions, and does it take longer?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the drawing come out better when the listener stays silent, or when the listener can ask questions? Which way will be quicker? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use four picture cards that are equally hard: each has the same 4 kinds of shapes in different places. The same person describes in rounds 1 and 2, and the other person describes in rounds 3 and 4. Use a clock to time each round. Score each drawing the same way, 2 points for each shape: 1 for the right shape and size, 1 for the right place. In rounds 1 and 2 the silent round comes first. In rounds 3 and 4, do the round with questions first, so practice does not favour one kind of round.

materials.item: 4 picture cards that you draw yourself (step 1 says how)
plain paper (4 sheets) and a pencil for the listener
2 chairs placed back to back
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: Draw 4 picture cards. Describe two pictures, one with a silent listener and one with questions allowed. Score and time both. Swap roles and repeat, with the questions round first.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Put each drawing next to its picture card.

setup.art: A card with four simple shapes on it: a big circle top left, a small square inside it, a triangle bottom right and a straight line joining them.
setup.caption: 1. The describer holds a picture card the listener must not see.

setup.art: A girl and an adult sitting on chairs back to back, the girl describing a card and the adult drawing on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Sit back to back. One describes, the other draws.

setup.art: Two drawings side by side next to their picture cards, with ticks and crosses on the shapes.
setup.caption: 3. Compare each drawing with its card. Score 2 points for each shape.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Words Only test. Here you set up the chairs and the picture cards.
flow.do: 1. Draw 4 picture cards and label them A, B, C and D. Each has the same 4 shapes: a circle, a square, a triangle and a straight line, in different sizes and places. 2. Put two chairs back to back. 3. The describer takes cards A and B, face down. The listener takes paper and a pencil. 4. Ask for guesses and reasons.
flow.say: You will describe a picture using only words. I will draw it without seeing it. First, guess. Will my drawing be better if I stay silent, or if I can ask questions? Why?
flow.kid: Sit back to back. Hide your pictures. Then say your guess and why.
flow.parent: Keep the shapes simple so the four cards are equally hard. Cards A and B are for the first two rounds. Cards C and D are for the swap.

flow.do: 1. Round 1: the describer describes picture A. 2. The listener draws and says nothing at all. 3. Time the round. 4. Stop when the describer says 'done'.
flow.say: Round 1. I must stay silent. I cannot ask anything. Describe picture A as clearly as you can. Tell me when you are done.
flow.kid: Describe picture A. Your listener must stay silent. Say 'done' at the end.
flow.parent: Do not nod, sigh or ask. This is one-way communication, like a radio programme.

flow.do: 1. Round 2: the describer describes picture B. 2. This time the listener may ask as many questions as they like. 3. Time the round.
flow.say: Round 2. Now I can ask questions. Describe picture B. I will ask whenever I am not sure.
flow.kid: Describe picture B. Now your listener can ask questions. Answer each one.
flow.parent: Ask real questions: 'How big is the circle?' 'Is the line touching the triangle?' This is two-way communication, like a phone call.

flow.do: 1. Turn the cards over. 2. Score each drawing: 2 points for each shape, 1 for the right shape and size, 1 for the right place. 3. Write the scores and times.
flow.say: Let's score them. For each shape, one point if it is the right shape and size, and one if it is in the right place.
flow.kid: Put each drawing next to its card. Give points for each shape. Write the scores and times.

ask.q: Which round had the higher score? Which was quicker?
good: The round with questions scored higher.
The silent round was quicker.

flow.do: 1. Swap roles: the person who described now listens and draws. 2. Use cards C and D. Do the round with questions first (card C), then the silent round (card D). 3. Score and time both.
flow.say: Now we swap. This time the round with questions comes first, then the silent round. Does the same thing happen?
flow.kid: Swap roles. Do the round with questions first, then the silent round. Score and time both.
flow.parent: Swapping roles and order checks that the result is not just because one of you describes better, or because the second go was easier.

flow.do: Ask your child what they found, what shows it, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: What did you find? What is your evidence? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Which way gave better drawings? Which was quicker? Why do you think so?

ask.q: A road sign cannot answer questions. What does that mean for how it must be made?
good: It must be very simple.
Everyone must understand it at once.
It uses shapes and pictures, not long words.

check.q: Which of these is two-way communication?
options: A phone call with a friend
check.why: On a phone call, both people can talk and ask questions. A road sign, a radio programme and a poster send a message only one way: you cannot answer them back.

activities.title: The Kitchen Journey: how far did our food travel?
activities.context: You will find out how far your kitchen packets travelled, and how they reached your home.

materials.item: 5 packets or things from the kitchen: rice, salt, tea, sugar, a soap, a fruit
a map of India, in a book or on a phone
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Read 5 packets. Find each place on the map. Guess how each one travelled to your home.

activities.record: Make a list: the thing, where it came from, and how you think it travelled.

setup.art: Five kitchen packets on a table, a child's finger pointing at the small print on a tea packet.
setup.caption: 1. Read where each packet was made or packed.

setup.art: A map of India with dotted lines from Assam, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh to a city in South India, with a truck, a train and a ship drawn on the lines.
setup.caption: 2. Find each place on the map. Say how it travelled.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Journey. You read where kitchen things come from.
flow.do: 1. Put 5 packets on the table. 2. Your child reads where each one was made or packed. 3. Find each place on the map.
flow.say: Almost nothing in our kitchen was made in our home. Let's read where these came from, and find each place on the map.
flow.kid: Read the small print on each packet. Where was it packed? Find the place on the map.

flow.do: 1. For each packet, ask how it reached your home. 2. Ask what the family would have if nothing could be carried from far away.
flow.say: How do you think this packet got from where it was made to our shop? And from the shop to our home? What would we have if nothing could travel?
flow.kid: For each packet, pick truck, train, ship or scooter. Then think about what we would eat if nothing could travel.

ask.q: How did this packet get to our home?
good: By truck from where it was made.
By train, then by the shop's van.
Someone carried it from the shop.

flow.parent: Good answers name more than one kind of transport, such as a train and then a truck. Tea often comes from the Nilgiris, Munnar or Assam. Salt often comes from Thoothukudi or Gujarat.

activities.title: The Time-line Rope: put transport and messages in order
activities.context: You will find out which came first, the boat or the wheel, and how messages grew from drums to phones. You put 12 cards in order on a string.

materials.item: a long string or a dupatta, laid across the floor
12 small paper cards and a pencil
clothes pegs or tape

schedule.what: Draw 12 cards of transport and messages. Peg them on a string in order. Check the order together.

activities.record: Take a photo of your time-line, or copy it into your notebook.

setup.art: Twelve small hand-drawn cards: a footpath, a log boat, a bullock cart, a steam train, an aeroplane, a metro, a drum, a pigeon, a letter, a telephone, a radio and a mobile phone.
setup.caption: 1. Write one thing on each card.

setup.art: A string stretched across a floor with the cards pegged on it in order from oldest to newest.
setup.caption: 2. Peg them on the string, oldest at one end.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Time-line Rope. You make 12 picture cards.
flow.do: 1. Write one thing on each of 12 cards. 2. Transport: a footpath, a log boat, a bullock cart, a steam train, a bus and an aeroplane. 3. Messages: a drum, a messenger pigeon, a letter, a telephone, a radio and a mobile phone.
flow.say: Let's write twelve ways people have travelled and sent messages, one on each card. A tiny picture is fine too.
flow.kid: Write one thing on each card. Add a tiny picture if you like.

flow.do: 1. Your child pegs the cards on the string in the order they think they were invented. 2. Then read the 'How transport grew' and 'How communication grew' cards together and fix the order.
flow.say: Put them in order, oldest at this end and newest at that end. Which do you think came first, the boat or the wheel?
flow.kid: Peg the cards in order. Oldest at one end. Newest at the other. Which came first, the boat or the wheel?
flow.parent: Boats came long before wheels. A log canoe found in the Netherlands is about 10,000 years old. The oldest wheels are about 5,500 years old. Messengers and drums came long before letters and the post.

flow.do: Ask what each new invention made possible.
flow.say: Pick one card. What could people do after this was invented that they could not do before?
flow.kid: Pick one card. What could people do after it was invented?

check.q: Which of these was invented first?
check.why: The telegraph came in the 1800s, before the telephone in 1876. Radio followed in the early 1900s, and mobile phones came to India in 1995.

flow.parent: Good answers name a real change. For example: after the wheel, animals could pull heavy loads instead of people carrying them. After the telephone, a family could talk to a relative in another town at once.

activities.title: Sign Spotting: read the road signs near home
activities.context: You will find out what the shapes of road signs tell you. You walk with a grown-up, spot signs near home, and sort them by shape.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a phone camera, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up holds the child's hand on the road. Stay on the footpath. Stop to look and draw only in a safe place, never at the road's edge.

schedule.what: Walk along a nearby road with a grown-up. Draw every road sign you see. Sort them into circles, triangles and rectangles at home.

activities.record: Keep a photo or a drawing of each sign you saw. Say or write what it means. Sort them into three groups: circles (orders), triangles (warnings) and rectangles (information).

setup.art: A grown-up and a child on a footpath, the child pointing at a round 'No horn' sign near a hospital gate.
setup.caption: 1. Walk on the footpath with a grown-up. Look for signs.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns, headed circle, triangle and rectangle, with small drawings of road signs in each.
setup.caption: 2. At home, sort your signs by shape.

flow.context: This is the first step of Sign Spotting. You walk with a grown-up and look for road signs.
flow.do: 1. Walk on the footpath along a busy road near home. 2. Stop in a safe place each time your child spots a sign or signal. 3. You photograph it, or your child draws it.
flow.say: Let's be sign spotters. Every time you see a road sign or a signal, tell me. We will stop somewhere safe to take a photo of it.
flow.kid: Hold the grown-up's hand. Look for road signs. Say 'sign!' when you see one.
flow.parent: Look near schools, hospitals, junctions, bus stops and speed breakers. Zebra crossings and the pedestrian lights at a signal count too.

flow.do: 1. At home, sort the signs into circles, triangles and rectangles. 2. Read the 'Road signs and traffic lights' card to check the meanings.
flow.say: Let's sort your signs by shape. What do all the circles have in common? What about the triangles?
flow.kid: Sort your signs into circles, triangles and rectangles. What does each shape mean?

ask.q: What does a red-bordered triangle tell a driver?
good: Be careful, something is ahead.
It is a warning.

activities.title: Torch Code: send a word across the room without a sound
activities.context: You will find out how a word can travel as a pattern of short and long flashes, like a message on the old telegraph. You invent a torch code and send a word across the room.

materials.item: a torch, or a phone torch
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes. Point it at the wall or the ceiling.

schedule.what: Make a code for 6 letters. Send a short word by torch flashes. Swap and try again.

activities.record: Write your code on a card. Write which words got through correctly and which did not.

setup.art: A card with six letters, each with a pattern of dots and dashes beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a code: a pattern of short and long flashes for each letter.

setup.art: A child in a dim room flashing a torch at the ceiling, and a parent across the room writing letters on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Flash a word at the ceiling. Your partner writes it down.

flow.context: This is the first step of Torch Code. You make a code of short and long flashes.
flow.do: 1. Together, choose 6 letters, such as A, E, I, P, T and N. 2. Give each one a different pattern of short and long flashes. 3. Both of you copy the code.
flow.say: Long ago, the telegraph sent messages as short and long pulses. We will make our own code with a torch. Give each letter its own pattern.
flow.kid: Pick six letters. Give each one a pattern. Short flash is a dot. Long flash is a dash.

flow.do: 1. Dim the lights. 2. Your child flashes a 3-letter word at the ceiling, such as PAN or TEN. 3. You write down the letters. 4. Swap.
flow.say: Flash your word at the ceiling. Wait a little between letters, so I know where one ends.
flow.kid: Flash your word at the ceiling. Pause between letters. Did your partner get it?

ask.q: What went wrong when a word did not get through?
good: The pause between letters was too short.
Two letters had codes that looked alike.

flow.do: Talk about how the real telegraph and today's phones send messages as patterns.
flow.say: The telegraph used a code like ours, called Morse code, sent along wires. Your phone still sends messages as patterns, much faster. What is good about a code? What is hard?
flow.kid: Your phone sends messages as fast patterns too. What was hard about your code?
flow.parent: In Morse code, the letter S is three short signals. It was the first letter Marconi reported hearing across the Atlantic in 1901.

activities.title: Window Traffic Count: how many people does each vehicle carry?
activities.context: You will find out which vehicle carries the most people. You watch the road from a window or balcony and count vehicles and the people inside them.

materials.item: a window or balcony that looks onto a road, or a safe spot at your gate with a grown-up
a tally sheet and a pencil

activities.safety: Stay well back from the balcony rail. A grown-up stays with you.

schedule.what: For 10 minutes, tally cars, two-wheelers, autos and buses, and count the people in each. Work out people per vehicle.

activities.record: Make a tally table: vehicle, how many passed, and how many people you counted in them.

setup.art: A child at a balcony with a grown-up, looking at a road with a bus, cars, two-wheelers and an auto.
setup.caption: 1. Watch the road for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A tally sheet with rows for car, two-wheeler, auto and bus, and tally marks for vehicles and for people.
setup.caption: 2. Tally each vehicle, and the people you can see inside.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Window Traffic Count. You tally vehicles and people for 10 minutes.
flow.do: 1. Set a timer for 10 minutes. 2. For each car, two-wheeler and auto, make a tally mark and count the people you can see. 3. For a bus, guess roughly how full it is.
flow.say: For ten minutes, let's count vehicles. For each one, also count the people in it. For a bus, guess if it is empty, half full or full.
flow.kid: Make a tally mark for each vehicle. Count the people in it. Is the bus full?
flow.parent: A full city bus can carry about 50 or more people. Your child cannot count them, so a rough guess is fine.

flow.do: Compare how many people each kind of vehicle carried, and how much road it took up.
flow.say: How many cars passed? How many people were in them? About how many cars take up as much road as one bus?
flow.kid: Which kind of vehicle carried the most people in all? Which carried the fewest people in each vehicle?

ask.q: Why might a city want more buses and fewer cars?
good: A bus carries many people in one vehicle.
Less smoke and less traffic for each person.

flow.parent: A car with only one person in it makes the most exhaust for each person. A full bus makes the least, because many people share one engine. That is why a city wants more people in each vehicle.

activities.title: Ask an Older Person: how did you travel and send messages at my age?
activities.context: You will find out how travel and messages changed in one lifetime. You ask a grandparent, an older relative or an older neighbour how they travelled and sent messages when they were young.

materials.item: a phone, or a visit
a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Interview an older person with 5 questions. Write down their answers. Compare their childhood with yours.

activities.record: Write a short 'then and now' table with their answers and yours.

setup.art: A girl on a video call with her grandmother, a notebook open on her lap.
setup.caption: 1. Call a grandparent and ask your questions.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns, 'Paati, then' and 'Me, now', and short answers about school, trains and letters.
setup.caption: 2. Write a 'then and now' table.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ask an Older Person. You interview an older person about travel and messages long ago.
flow.do: 1. Help your child write 5 questions. 2. Your child asks them on the phone or in person. 3. They write short answers.
flow.say: Ask: How did you get to school? What was your first train journey? How did you send news to relatives? When did you first use a phone? When did you first watch TV?
flow.kid: Ask your five questions. Listen well. Write a few words for each answer.
flow.parent: Many grandparents in India remember telegrams for urgent news, postcards, long-distance trunk calls booked through the telephone exchange, and the first TV in the street.

flow.do: Fill in the 'then and now' table together.
flow.say: Let's compare. What is faster now? Is anything better about how it was then?
flow.kid: Fill in your table. What is faster now? Was anything better then?

activities.title: Vehicle Picture Book: draw or collect vehicles
activities.context: You will make a small picture book of vehicles. You draw some, or cut pictures from old papers, and write what each one runs on.

materials.item: old newspapers or magazines
paper, scissors, glue and pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with scissors and any outing.

schedule.what: Draw or cut out six vehicles. Stick them in a book. Under each, write its kind of transport and its fuel.

activities.record: Keep the book. Count how many vehicles use petrol, diesel, CNG or electricity.

setup.art: A child cutting a bus picture from a newspaper, with a paper book and glue.
setup.caption: 1. Draw or cut out six vehicles.

setup.art: A page with one vehicle stuck and a line beneath it: 'Road. Diesel.'
setup.caption: 2. Write the kind of transport and the fuel.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Vehicle Picture Book. You find six vehicles.
flow.do: 1. Cut six vehicles from old papers or draw them. 2. Try to find different kinds: a cycle, a bus, a train, a boat, an aeroplane and an e-rickshaw.
flow.say: Let's find six different vehicles. Draw them or cut them out.
flow.kid: Find or draw six different vehicles.

flow.do: 1. Stick each vehicle on a page. 2. Write its kind of transport and what fuel it uses.
flow.say: What does each one run on? Petrol, diesel, CNG, electricity or just legs?
flow.kid: Write what each vehicle runs on.
flow.parent: A cycle runs on the rider's legs. An e-rickshaw runs on a battery. Many city buses use diesel or CNG.

activities.title: Letter and Call: send the same news two ways
activities.context: You will show two ways to send news: a letter and a call. You find out which is quicker and what is good about each.

materials.item: paper, envelope and pencil
a phone, with a grown-up's help

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with scissors and any outing.

schedule.what: Write a short letter to a relative and put it in an envelope. Then, with a grown-up, call them with the same news.

activities.record: Write one line: which was quicker, and what is good about each.

setup.art: A child writing a letter with an envelope on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Write a letter and put it in an envelope.

setup.art: A child on a phone call with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Call with the same news.

flow.context: This is the first step. You write a letter and make a call with the same news.
flow.do: 1. Write two lines to a relative. 2. Put it in an envelope and address it with the PIN code. 3. Then call the same relative, with a grown-up's help, and tell them the same news.
flow.say: Let's send the same news two ways. First a letter, then a call.
flow.kid: Write a short letter. Then say the same news on a call.

flow.do: Ask which way was quicker, and which one can be kept.
flow.say: Which one reached them first? Which can they keep and read again?
flow.kid: Which was quicker? Which can be kept?
flow.parent: A call is quick. A letter takes days, but can be kept and read again. Both are good, and each fits a different need.

projects.title: Our Safe Walk Map: the route to the nearest shop
projects.context: You will find out where the walk to the shop is safe and where it is not. In this 2-day project you walk the route with a grown-up, then make a map of the safe crossings, the signs and the dark places.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a large sheet of paper and coloured pencils
a torch, for the evening walk

projects.safety: A grown-up walks with the child both times and holds their hand at crossings. Do the evening walk before it is fully dark.

schedule.what: Walk to the shop in daylight. Note the crossings, signs and signals. Note where the footpath is broken or missing.
Walk the same route at dusk with a torch. Note the dark places. Draw the map with symbols and a key.

projects.record: Draw the map, or lay it out with small objects and take a photo. Use a symbol for each crossing, sign, signal and dark spot, and explain them in a key.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up on a footpath, the child writing in a notebook next to a zebra crossing.
setup.caption: 1. Walk the route in daylight. Note every crossing and sign.

setup.art: The same street at dusk, the child shining a torch at the ground and pointing at a dark corner without a street light.
setup.caption: 2. Walk it again at dusk. Find the dark places.

setup.art: A hand-drawn map with a home, a shop, zebra stripes, small sign symbols, black dots for dark spots, and a key in the corner.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the map with a key.

flow.context: This is day 1 of the Safe Walk Map. You walk to the shop in daylight and note what keeps walkers safe.
flow.do: 1. Walk to the nearest shop with your child. 2. At each crossing, signal or sign, stop and let your child note it. 3. Note where walkers must step onto the road.
flow.say: Today we are road checkers. Where are the safe places to cross? Where must we walk on the road? Let's note them all.
flow.kid: Hold hands. Note every crossing, signal and sign. Where is there no footpath?

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Safe Walk Map. You walk the same route at dusk.
flow.do: 1. Walk the same route at dusk, with a torch. 2. Note dark spots with no street light. 3. Notice which walkers you see easily.
flow.say: Now it is getting dark. Where can drivers not see us well? Which people on the road can you see easily, and why?
flow.kid: Shine the torch at the ground. Where is it darkest? Who is easy to see?
flow.wait: Do this on day 2, at dusk.

flow.do: Make the map with a key, at home. Draw it, or lay it out on the floor with small objects and take a photo.
flow.say: Let's draw the map. Make a symbol for crossings, signals, signs and dark spots, and put them in a key.
flow.kid: Show your home and the shop. Add the crossings, signs and dark spots. Make a key. Draw them, or use small objects and take a photo.

ask.q: If a friend walked this way at night, what would you tell them?
good: Cross at the zebra crossing.
Wear something white and carry a torch.
Be careful at the dark corner.

challenges.title: A Sign Without Words
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design a sign that everyone understands at once, even someone who cannot read.
challenges.problem: Your building needs a sign at the gate that says: 'Children play here. Drive slowly.' Some visitors and drivers do not read the languages used in your area. Design a sign that anyone understands in two seconds.
constraints: It must be understood in 2 seconds, from 5 steps away.
Use the shape and colour rules that road signs use.
general: Use a triangle with a red border, because a triangle means a warning.
Draw two running children in black, like the real 'School ahead' sign.
Add a red circle with '10' to give a speed limit.
creative: Test the sign on three people: show it for two seconds, then ask what it means.
Make it bigger and simpler after each test.
If you have reflective tape, stick a strip on the border so it shines in headlights.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sign for something in your building or street. Show it for 2 seconds to three people. Did they all understand it?

setup.art: A child drawing a red-bordered triangle with two running children on a sheet of card.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a sign with no words.

setup.art: The child holding the sign up for two seconds while an adult, five steps away, guesses its meaning.
setup.caption: 2. Show it for 2 seconds from 5 steps away. Do people understand?

flow.do: Your child makes three sign ideas, by sketching them or cutting them from coloured paper. Use shapes and colours from real road signs.
flow.say: A driver has two seconds to read your sign. What shape should it be? What picture? Make three ideas.
flow.kid: Sketch three ideas, or cut them from coloured paper. Say why you chose each shape and colour.

flow.do: Show the best sign to three people for 2 seconds each, from 5 steps away. Write what they say.
flow.say: Hold it up for just two seconds. Then ask, 'What does it mean?'
flow.kid: Show your sign for two seconds. Ask what it means. Write their answers.

flow.do: Improve the sign and test again.
flow.say: What confused people? How can you make it simpler?
flow.kid: Fix what confused people. Test it again.

check.q: Which shape should a warning sign be, in India?
check.why: In India, a triangle with a red border warns drivers of something ahead. Circles give orders and rectangles give information.

challenges.title: Be Seen: a night band for a school bag
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You make a band for a school bag that drivers can see from far away at night, using things from home.
challenges.problem: A child walks home from tuition after dark. Make a band for their school bag that a driver can see from as far away as possible, using only things from home. Test it with the dim torch from the Seen in the Dark test.
constraints: It must not fall off when the bag is shaken.
Test it in the dark with the dim torch held next to your eye, and count foot-steps.
materials: a steel lid or an old CD
the dim torch from the Seen in the Dark test
general: Use a strip of white cloth: white reflects much more light than dark colours.
If you have reflective tape, use it: it sends light back towards the driver.
Make the band wide: a bigger white area is seen from further away.
creative: Crumple kitchen foil, then smooth it flat, so it glints from many angles.
Cut an old CD into strips with a grown-up's help: it shines in many directions.
Put bands on both the front and the back, so drivers coming either way can see them.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own night band. Test it in the dark. How many foot-steps away can you still see it? Can you beat the white cloth?

setup.art: A school bag with a band of white cloth and crumpled foil taped across it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a band from white cloth, foil or other shiny things.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding a dim torch by her eye, stepping back from a chair with the school bag on it.
setup.caption: 2. Test it with the dim torch. Count foot-steps.

flow.do: Your child chooses materials and makes a band for the bag.
flow.say: In the Seen in the Dark test, which cloth did you see from furthest away? Use that to design your band.
flow.kid: Pick your materials and make the band.
flow.parent: Help with scissors. If you cut a CD, a grown-up does the cutting, because the edges can be sharp.

flow.do: Test the band in the dark. Hold the dim torch next to your eye, as in the Seen in the Dark test. Count foot-steps.
flow.say: Let's test it in the dark. Step back until you can't see the band. How far?
flow.kid: Test your band in the dark. Count your foot-steps. Did it beat the white cloth?

flow.do: Talk about what worked best and why.
flow.say: Which part of your band shone furthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Point to the part that shone furthest.

quiz.p: Which kind of transport is a goods train?
quiz.why: A train runs on rails, so it is rail transport.

quiz.p: Which came first in history?
quiz.why: Boats are about 10,000 years old or more. Trains, cars and aeroplanes are all less than 250 years old.

quiz.p: A child will walk home after dark. Which clothes help drivers see the child from furthest away?
opts: A white frock with a reflective strip on the bag
quiz.why: White reflects much more of a car's headlight than dark colours, and a reflective strip sends the light straight back to the driver. A driver sees a person only by the light that comes back from them, and dark clothes send back very little.

quiz.p: What does a red-bordered triangle on a road sign tell a driver?
quiz.why: In India, a triangle with a red border is a warning sign, such as 'School ahead' or 'Speed breaker'.

quiz.p: The traffic light shows amber. What should a driver do?
quiz.why: Amber means the light is about to turn red, so get ready to stop.

quiz.p: Which of these is one-way communication?
quiz.why: You can listen to a radio programme, but you cannot ask it questions. The other three are two-way.

quiz.p: A road sign is a blue circle with a white arrow pointing straight up. What does it tell a driver?
quiz.why: A blue circle gives an order about what you must do. This one says to go straight only.

quiz.p: Which of these makes no exhaust at all?
quiz.why: A cycle burns no fuel, so it makes no exhaust. Petrol and diesel engines give out smoke and gases.

quiz.p: What is the cheapest way to carry very heavy goods across the sea?
quiz.why: Ships carry huge loads cheaply, though slowly. Aeroplanes are fast but cost far more.

quiz.p: Which invention first sent messages as electric pulses along wires?
quiz.why: The telegraph sent short and long pulses of electricity along wires, in a code such as Morse code.

quiz.p: A sign is a red circle with '30' inside. What does it mean?
opts: Do not go faster than 30 kilometres an hour
quiz.why: A red circle gives an order. A number inside it is a speed limit in kilometres an hour.

quiz.p: One full bus carries about as many people as 25 cars. Why is that good for the city's air?
opts: One engine burns far less fuel than 25 engines
quiz.why: One bus engine burns much less fuel than 25 car engines. So sharing a bus makes much less smoke for each person.

quiz.p: Which of these fuels is a gas, squeezed into a tank?
quiz.why: CNG means compressed natural gas. Petrol and diesel are liquids.

quiz.p: A bus is stuck behind a long line of vehicles at a busy crossing. Which helps most to ease the jam?
opts: A flyover that lifts traffic over the crossing
More parked cars on the road
quiz.why: A flyover lets many vehicles go over the crossing without stopping. Horns and parked cars do not help, and a narrower road makes the jam worse.

quiz.p: Which one cuts both smoke and noise from vehicles?
opts: Switching the engine off at a long red light
quiz.why: An engine that is off makes no smoke and no noise. Horns and a badly kept engine make both worse.

quiz.p: An ambulance comes up behind you with its siren on. What should the drivers do?
opts: Move aside and let it pass
Stop in the middle of the road
quiz.why: An ambulance may be carrying someone in danger. Drivers must make way.

quiz.p: Who helps fix a bus engine so that it runs safely?
quiz.why: A mechanic mends engines. A porter carries bags, a conductor sells tickets, and a postman brings letters.

quiz.p: You want to cross a road in India. What should you do?
opts: Stop at the edge, look right, left and right again, and cross when it is clear
Wait in the middle of the road
quiz.why: Vehicles keep to the left in India, so the first danger comes from the right. Look both ways and hold a grown-up's hand.

quiz.p: On a hill bus, why must you keep your hands and head inside?
opts: The bus may pass very close to rocks, trees and other vehicles round a hairpin bend
The windows are for looking at the sky
quiz.why: On narrow hill roads, things pass very close. A head or hand outside can be hurt.

quiz.p: A sign shows a triangle with a red border and a picture of men digging. What does it mean?
quiz.why: A red-bordered triangle is a warning. This one tells drivers that people are working on the road ahead.

quiz.p: Which place is safest for a child to play?
opts: A park, with a grown-up nearby
quiz.why: A busy road has fast vehicles, a roof with no rail can lead to a fall, and a building site has holes and heavy machines.

quiz.p: Who rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road in the 1500s, with trees and rest houses along it?
quiz.why: Sher Shah Suri, a ruler in the 1500s, rebuilt this very old road across north India with trees, wells and rest houses.

quiz.p: Which was used for early water transport, before big ships?
quiz.why: Water transport started with small fishing boats. Later, bigger ships carried trade between countries.

quiz.p: Why can a helicopter be useful in a hill place such as Tawang?
opts: It can reach where roads are hard to build
quiz.why: Air transport can reach far hill places. It costs a lot and uses fuel, and a helicopter is loud.

quiz.p: Which of these did people use first to print words?
quiz.why: In China, people carved words into wood, inked them and pressed paper on them. Metal letters and computers came later.

quiz.p: A letter goes from Chennai to Kolkata. What happens between the postbox and the door?
opts: It is sorted by region and sent on by train or truck, and then a postman brings it
It goes straight to the door
quiz.why: Post office workers sort letters by PIN code and send them on. A postman delivers them at the end.

quiz.p: Which pair of dates is right for India?
quiz.why: Radio began in the 1920s and Doordarshan in 1959. The postal department began in 1854.

quiz.p: What did a teleprinter do?
opts: Sent typed messages along wires and printed them on paper
quiz.why: A teleprinter was a keyboard machine that printed typed messages at the far end.

quiz.p: What does teletext show?
opts: Pages of written news and weather on the TV screen
quiz.why: Teletext sent written pages along with the TV signal.

quiz.p: A farmer gets the price of onions in the mandi by SMS. Why is that useful?
opts: He can choose where to sell
quiz.why: Knowing the price helps him sell where he gets a fair price.

quiz.p: You get a message that says a big cyclone will hit tomorrow, but it came from a stranger. What is the best thing to do?
opts: Forward it to everyone at once
Check with a grown-up and a trusted news source first
Believe it because it is on a phone
quiz.why: False news can spread fast. Check who sent it and whether it is true before you share it.

quiz.p: Which of these is a good use of a phone and a bad use?
opts: Good: a call to a grandparent. Bad: staring at it all night
Good: staring at it all night. Bad: a call to a grandparent
quiz.why: A phone is useful for talking to family. Using it too much and losing sleep is a bad use.

worksheets.title: Transport, messages and road safety (core)
worksheets.context: This worksheet checks the main ideas: kinds of transport, road signs, one-way and two-way messages, and being seen at night.

items.p: Here is a list of ways to travel. Sort each one into its kind of transport.
items.a: see items
items.why: Road transport runs on roads, rail on tracks, water transport floats, and air transport flies. A kattumaram is a raft of logs tied together. A strong answer knows that a metro is rail transport, even when it runs on a bridge above the road.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, the same dim torch shines on a black cloth and a white cloth. Which one can you still see from further away?
items.why: The white cloth reflects much more of the torch light back to your eyes, so you can still see it from further away. The black cloth reflects very little, so it vanishes sooner.

items.p: Someone says, 'I can see the car's headlights, so the driver can see me.' Explain why this may be wrong.
items.a: The person sees the bright lamp itself. The driver sees the person only by the little light that bounces off them and comes back. If the person wears dark clothes, very little light comes back, so the driver may not see them.
items.why: A strong answer says that seeing a lamp and being seen by its light are different. It uses the idea of light bouncing off and coming back.

items.p: A traffic light that is ____ means stop.
items.why: Red means stop, amber means get ready to stop, and green means go.

items.p: Match each road sign shape to what it tells you.
pairs: useful information, such as the way to a petrol pump
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In India, circles give orders, triangles warn, and rectangles give information. A strong answer could draw one example of each.

items.p: Boats were invented long before wheels.
items.why: Log canoes about 10,000 years old have been found. The oldest wheels are about 5,500 years old. Many people guess the wheel came first.

items.p: Draw a road sign that warns drivers that a school is ahead. Colour its border.
items.a: A triangle with a red border, a white middle, and two children drawn in black.
items.why: A warning sign is a red-bordered triangle. The picture of children tells drivers to slow down and watch out.

items.p: Which of these is two-way communication?
items.why: In a talk, both of you can speak and ask questions. A newspaper, a billboard and TV news send a message one way only.

items.p: Put these ways of sending messages in order, from oldest to newest.
items.why: Messengers on foot are thousands of years old. The telegraph came in the 1800s, radio in the early 1900s, and mobile phones in India in 1995.

items.p: Name two ways that cars and buses harm the air or our health.
items.a: Their exhaust has tiny specks of soot and harmful gases that hurt our lungs. It also has carbon dioxide, which warms the Earth. Horns and engines make noise pollution too.
items.why: A strong answer names two different harms, such as dirty air and noise, or harm to lungs and warming of the Earth.

items.p: You want to send a photo to a cousin in Kolkata right now. Which is the quickest way?
opts: Send it by phone over the internet
Give it to a train passenger
items.why: The internet carries a photo in seconds. A letter or courier takes days.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai are going to a shop 1 kilometre away, on a hot afternoon.

views.says: We should walk. It makes no smoke and no noise, and it is good exercise.
We should take an auto. It is hot, and it is faster.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as no pollution, or saving time in the heat. It also gives the other friend their due: walking is clean and healthy, and an auto is quicker and easier in great heat or with heavy bags.
items.why: There is a real trade-off between clean travel and quick, comfortable travel. A good answer weighs both.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a means of communication?
items.why: A bullock cart carries people and goods. It is transport. Letters, phone calls and radio carry messages.

items.p: Label the three lights of a traffic signal with what each one means.
items.why: The red light is at the top, amber in the middle and green at the bottom. A strong answer writes what each colour tells the driver to do.
items.art: A traffic signal with three empty circles.

items.p: Your family walks home after dinner at night. Write two things each person can do so that drivers see them.
items.a: Wear white or pale clothes. Wear or carry something with a reflective strip. Carry a torch and shine it on the ground ahead.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Seen in the Dark test: pale clothes and reflective strips send much more light back to a driver.

items.p: Match each person to what they do for transport.
pairs: carries heavy bags at a station
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Many people work so that transport runs well. A strong answer can name one more job, such as a pilot or a boatman.

items.p: Draw or paste four pictures of different vehicles. Write under each one what fuel it uses: petrol, diesel, CNG or electricity.
items.a: Four pictures, such as a bus (diesel or CNG), a scooter (petrol), an e-rickshaw (electricity) and a car, each with a fuel written below.
items.why: A strong answer picks four different vehicles and names a fuel for each. A cycle uses no fuel at all, only the rider's legs.
items.art: Four empty boxes in a row.

items.p: On a bus it is safe to put your hand out of the window.
items.why: Your hand or head can hit a pole, a tree or another vehicle. Keep them inside and sit down.

items.p: Match each sign to what it tells you.
pairs: do not leave your vehicle here
a bump is ahead, so slow down
people are working, so go slowly
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These signs use words as well as pictures. A strong answer could draw one new sign of their own.

items.p: What is email?
opts: A message sent by the internet
items.why: Email is a message sent by the internet from one person to another, in seconds.

worksheets.title: Signs, signals and choices (stretch)
worksheets.context: This worksheet goes further: reflective signs, one-way messages, choosing transport, and how radio crosses the Earth.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, a reflective strip on the chair shone brightly when the torch was beside your eye. What happened when you held the torch far out to the side?
items.why: A reflective strip sends light straight back towards the lamp. With the torch by your eye, the light came straight back to you. With the torch to the side, the light went back to the torch, not to your eyes.

items.p: Many road signs are covered with reflective sheeting. Why does this help a driver at night?
items.a: The sheeting sends the car's headlight straight back towards the driver. So the sign shines brightly to the driver, even though no lamp is switched on inside it.
items.why: A strong answer says where the light comes from (the car's own headlights) and where it goes (back to the driver).

items.p: In the Words Only test, one person describes a picture and the other draws it. In one round the listener stays silent. In another round the listener may ask questions. In which round does the drawing probably score higher?
opts: When the listener had to stay silent
When the listener could ask questions
Scores have nothing to do with questions
items.why: When the listener can ask, they can clear up mistakes, such as which shape is bigger. Two-way communication usually gets more right, but it takes longer.

items.p: A driver passes a road sign in two seconds. Use what you found in the Words Only test (a listener who cannot ask questions made more mistakes) to explain why a road sign must be very simple.
items.a: A road sign is one-way communication. The driver cannot ask it what it means. In the test, the silent listener made more mistakes. So a sign must be simple enough to understand at once, with no questions.
items.why: A strong answer links the sign to one-way communication and uses evidence from the test.

items.p: Sort these into one-way and two-way communication.
items.a: see items
items.why: In two-way communication, both sides can send and receive. Letters sent back and forth are two-way, but slow.

items.p: Which is the best way to carry petrol from a refinery to a city 300 kilometres away, every day, for years?
items.why: A pipeline carries liquid all day and night, without any vehicle. Once it is built, it is cheap and safe for this job.

items.p: Electric scooters give out no exhaust on the road, but their electricity may still cause pollution somewhere else.
items.why: In India, much electricity is made by burning coal in power stations. So the pollution moves from the road to the power station.

items.p: A town council in Kerala is deciding how to spend money on transport.

views.says: Build a wider road, so more cars can come to the market.
Build footpaths and cycle lanes, so people walk and cycle, and the air is cleaner.
Run more buses, so people without cars can travel too.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose? Give two reasons. Then say what is good about one of the other plans.
items.a: A strong answer chooses a plan and gives two reasons, such as clean air, cost, or who can use it. It then fairly names a strength of another plan, for example that a wider road helps trucks bring goods to shops.
items.why: Real towns weigh these trade-offs. More road space often fills with more cars. Footpaths and buses help people without cars. There is no single right answer.

items.p: The 6-digit number in an Indian address that helps the post office sort letters is called the ____.
items.why: PIN stands for Postal Index Number. PIN codes began in India in 1972.

items.p: Draw a map of a road crossing near a school. Put a zebra crossing, a 'School ahead' sign and a traffic light where they should go.
items.a: A crossroads with zebra stripes at the crossing near the school gate, a red-bordered triangle with children placed before the school on each side, and a traffic light at the junction.
items.why: Warning signs must come before the danger, so drivers have time to slow down. A strong drawing puts the sign some way before the school, not at its gate.
items.art: A blank outline of two crossing roads and a school building.

items.p: Radio waves travel in straight lines. Yet a radio station far beyond the curve of the Earth can sometimes be heard. Why?
opts: Radio waves curl around the Earth by themselves
A charged layer high in the air sends some radio waves back down
Radio waves travel through the ground
items.why: The ionosphere, a layer of charged air high above us, sends some radio waves back down to the ground. Edward Appleton showed this in 1924.

items.p: Choose one invention from this lesson: the wheel, the train, the telegraph or the mobile phone. What could people do after it that they could not do before?
items.a: For example: after the train, people could travel across India in days instead of weeks, and carry heavy goods like coal and rice cheaply to faraway cities.
items.why: A strong answer names a real change and says why the invention made it possible.

items.p: Put these ways of sending a message to a cousin in another state in order, from slowest to fastest.
items.why: A letter takes days. A telegram took hours, and the last one was sent in 2013. A WhatsApp message arrives in seconds.

items.p: Three of these are warning signs. Which is the odd one out?
opts: A triangle with a speed breaker
A triangle with a sharp bend
A red circle with a crossed-out horn
items.why: The red circle is an order: do not sound your horn. The triangles all warn of something ahead.

items.p: A honeybee finds flowers and comes back to the hive. How does she tell other bees where the flowers are?
opts: She dances, and the direction and length of her dance show the way
She buzzes the name of the flower
items.why: Honeybees dance on the comb. The direction of the dance shows which way to fly, and its length shows how far. Karl von Frisch worked this out.

items.p: Name two reasons for a traffic jam, and give one way to make it smaller.
items.a: Reasons: too many vehicles at once, a narrow road, a vehicle that broke down. A way to reduce it: build a flyover, run more buses, or share rides.
items.why: A strong answer gives two real reasons and one way that fits those reasons.

items.p: Which road runs across north India and was rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri in the 1500s?
items.why: The Grand Trunk Road is very old. Sher Shah Suri rebuilt it and added trees, wells and rest houses.

items.p: Match each tool to what it does.
pairs: shows written news on a TV screen
copies a page and prints it far away
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each tool carries a message in its own way. Only radio and TV send their message through the air to many homes.

items.p: Write one good use and one bad use of a phone, a letter or TV.
items.a: Good use: a phone call lets a child hear a grandparent far away. Bad use: a false message that spreads fast. A letter is slow but can be kept. TV can inform us, but too much watching wastes time.
items.why: A strong answer gives one fair good use and one fair bad use of the same tool.

items.p: Sort each into 'helps cut smoke and noise' or 'adds smoke and noise'.
items: switching off the engine at a red light
blowing the horn all the time
items.a: see items
items.why: Less fuel burnt and fewer horns means cleaner air and a quieter street.

worksheets.title: Thinking like a road engineer (challenge)
worksheets.context: This worksheet asks you to plan tests, weigh trade-offs and argue from evidence.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, the white cloth was seen from much further away than the black cloth. On a real road, why does this distance matter so much to a driver going fast?
items.a: A fast vehicle needs a long distance to slow down and stop. If the driver sees a walker only when very close, there is no time to stop. Seeing someone from further away gives the driver time.
items.why: A strong answer links seeing distance to stopping distance, and so to safety.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, suppose your white cloth is still visible at the far wall, 15 foot-steps away. What should you do to find how far it can really be seen?
opts: Make the torch dimmer, or use a longer room, and test all the cloths again
Test only the white cloth again
items.why: If the white cloth is still seen at the wall, you have not found its limit. A dimmer torch or a longer room lets you find it. You must test every cloth again in the same way, so the test stays fair.

items.p: After the Seen in the Dark test, three people talk about road safety at night.

views.says: Walkers must wear pale clothes and reflective strips. Then drivers will see them.
Drivers must slow down at night, because they cannot see everyone, whatever they wear.
The town must put up street lights and footpaths, so people do not walk on dark roads at all.

items.ask: Who do you think has the most important point? Use evidence from your test. Then explain why the other two still matter.
items.a: A strong answer uses the test, for example that the black cloth vanished at a few steps. It may choose any person, but it sees that all three help: being seen, driving slowly, and safer roads work together.
items.why: Road safety depends on walkers, drivers and the town together. A good answer weighs each.

items.p: Many people think bright neon colours are best at night. Plan a test in a dark room to check this. Say what you would compare, and what would make it fair.
items.a: I would compare a neon green or orange cloth with a white cloth and a reflective strip, using the dim torch by my eye. Same chair, same darkness, same torch, two tries each. I would count foot-steps until each vanished.
items.why: A strong plan keeps everything the same except the cloth, and tries each one more than once.

items.p: A traffic light shows amber for a few seconds between green and red. Why is the amber light there? What could happen without it?
items.a: Amber warns drivers that red is coming, so they can slow down and stop in time. A vehicle going fast cannot stop at once. Without amber, a driver could be in the middle of the junction when the light turned red, and crash into traffic coming the other way.
items.why: A strong answer links the warning to the time and distance a vehicle needs to stop.

items.p: A cyclone warning goes out by radio and TV. Is that one-way or two-way communication? What problem could that cause, and how could it be fixed?
items.a: It is one-way. People cannot ask questions, such as 'Where is the nearest shelter?' It could be fixed by giving a phone helpline, or by local volunteers who go to each street and answer questions.
items.why: A strong answer names it as one-way and suggests adding a two-way channel.

items.p: Marconi was the only person who worked on early radio.
items.why: Many people worked on radio. In Kolkata in the 1890s, J.C. Bose made and detected very short radio waves. Tesla, Popov and others also built radio devices.

items.p: Draw the curved Earth with two radio towers far apart. Show how a radio wave can travel from one to the other by bouncing off the ionosphere.
items.a: A curved Earth, a layer above it marked ionosphere, and a zigzag line from one tower up to the layer, down to the ground, and up and down again to the far tower.
items.why: A strong drawing shows straight lines that change direction at the ionosphere, not a wave that curves by itself.
items.art: A curved line for the Earth's surface with two small towers far apart.

items.p: Sacks of rice go from a farm in Andhra Pradesh to a shop in Kerala. Which two kinds of transport are most likely to carry them?
opts: A goods train, then a truck
items.why: Rice is heavy and travels a long way, so a goods train is cheap. A truck then takes it from the station to the shop door. Most goods use more than one kind of transport.

items.p: The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago, but in some hilly places people kept carrying loads on their backs or on animals for thousands of years more. Why might wheels not help much there?
items.a: Wheels need smooth, fairly flat ground or roads. On steep, rocky paths a cart cannot go, but a person or a donkey can.
items.why: A strong answer sees that an invention helps only where its conditions are right.

items.p: Sort each change by whether it would make city air cleaner or dirtier.
items.a: see items
items.why: Fewer engines burning fuel for each person means cleaner air. Jams and idling engines burn fuel without going anywhere.

items.p: A message travelling from Earth to a faraway spacecraft takes about a day to arrive. What does this mean for talking to it?
opts: You can chat with it like a phone call
Every question takes about two days to get an answer
items.why: The question takes about a day to get there and the answer about a day to come back. So conversation is very slow, more like letters than a phone call.

items.p: Some biologists say plants communicate when they release smells that warn their neighbours. Others prefer the word 'signalling'. What do you think counts as communication? Give a reason.
items.a: A strong answer gives a clear view and a reason, for example: 'It is communication, because one plant sends a message and another plant acts on the message, just like a crow's warning call.'
items.why: There is a real debate about the words. A good answer says what it thinks communication needs: a sender, a message and a receiver who acts.

items.p: Label the parts of a message's journey on a phone call.
a: radio waves reach a phone tower
the tower sends it on through cables or a satellite
it reaches another tower and then your friend's phone
items.why: A phone call is carried as radio waves to the nearest tower, then on through cables or satellites, then out again by radio to the other phone. A strong answer puts the parts in the right order.
items.art: Two phones far apart with a tower near each, and a cable and a satellite between the towers.

items.p: Put these steps of a letter's journey in order.
items: A postwoman brings it to the door
You post it in a post box
It goes by train or van to the right city
It is sorted by PIN code at a sorting office
a: You post it in a post box
It is sorted by PIN code at a sorting office
It goes by train or van to the right city
A postwoman brings it to the door
items.why: A letter is collected, sorted by PIN code, carried to the right area, and then delivered. Transport and communication work together here.

items.p: Put these Indian dates in order, from earliest to latest.
items.why: The post came first, then the telegraph, then radio and TV.

items.p: A message says, 'Free phones for everyone! Click here.' What is the best first step?
opts: Ask a grown-up and check who sent it
items.why: A message that offers free things may be a trick. Stop, ask and check, and do not share it.

items.p: A flyover costs a lot, but a bus lane costs less. Which would you choose for a busy crossing in your town? Give two reasons.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives two reasons, such as saving time, fewer jams, cost, or carrying more people in fewer vehicles. It names one good point of the other choice.
items.why: Both can ease a jam in different ways, and the best choice depends on the road.

items.p: On a hill road, a hairpin bend is a very sharp turn, so the bus goes slowly round it.
items.why: A hairpin bend is shaped like a hairpin. The bus slows down, and children stay seated.

applications: Reflective strips on school bags, helmets, uniforms of traffic police and cycle pedals keep people visible at night.
Road signs with reflective sheeting light up in headlights without any electricity.
Zebra crossings and pedestrian signals let people on foot cross safely.
Goods trains and ships carry food, coal and fuel across India and the world.
Pipelines bring drinking water, petrol and cooking gas to cities.
Phone alerts, radio and TV warn people when a cyclone is coming.
Ambulances have the word AMBULANCE written back to front on the front. A driver ahead then sees the word the right way round in their mirror.
Metros and buses carry many people with less smoke for each person.
Satellites pass on TV, phone and weather signals across India.
PIN codes help post offices sort millions of letters and parcels.

spotted.art: The back of a cycle at night with a glowing red reflector.

open_questions.q: Who really sent the first radio signals, and who deserves the most credit?
open_questions.why_open: Bose, Marconi, Tesla, Popov and others all did important early work at about the same time. Historians still argue about how to share the credit.

open_questions.q: Did Marconi really hear the signal across the Atlantic in 1901?
open_questions.why_open: Only Marconi and his assistant heard the faint clicks, and nothing was recorded. Some engineers have argued that he may have heard noise. Later tests by his company did work across the ocean.

open_questions.q: How can our cities move everyone quickly without dirtying the air?
open_questions.why_open: Metros, buses, electric vehicles, cycle lanes and working from home all help, but every city is different and nobody has found one answer that works everywhere.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do nearby plants respond to the warning smells of a plant being eaten?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that neighbours get their defences ready, but they are still working out which smells matter and how plants sense them.

open_questions.q: Where did the wheel first come from?

maths.problem: In the Seen in the Dark test, a white shirt was still seen from 15 foot-steps away. A black T-shirt vanished at 3 foot-steps. How many times further away was the white shirt seen?
maths.explain: The white shirt was seen at 15 foot-steps and the black T-shirt at 3. 15 divided by 3 is 5. So the white shirt was seen 5 times further away. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15.
maths.context: This is about the Seen in the Dark test. In a dark room, you step back from a cloth with a dim torch until the cloth vanishes.

chart.title: How far away each cloth could be seen

maths.why_maths: Saying 'five times further' tells a driver much more than saying 'white is better'.

maths.problem: In the Seen in the Dark test, a yellow dupatta was seen at 12 foot-steps on try 1 and 14 foot-steps on try 2. What is the average of the two tries? The average is the number exactly in the middle of the two.
maths.explain: 12 + 14 = 26. Half of 26 is 13. So the average is 13 foot-steps. It is the number exactly in the middle of the two tries.
maths.context: This is about the Seen in the Dark test, where each cloth is tested twice.
maths.why_maths: Two tries rarely give the same number. Taking the average gives one fair number for each cloth.

maths.problem: You watch the road for 10 minutes. You count 20 cars with 2 people in each, and 1 bus with about 40 people. Which carried more people: all the cars together, or the one bus?
maths.answer: They carried the same number: 40 people each.
maths.explain: 20 cars with 2 people each is 20 × 2 = 40 people. The bus carried about 40 people too. So one bus carried as many people as 20 cars, using one engine instead of 20.
maths.context: This is about the Window Traffic Count, where you count vehicles and the people in them.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how many people each kind of vehicle really carries, so you can compare them fairly.

maths.problem: India's first passenger train ran in 1853. Kochi's water metro began in 2023. How many years apart are they?
maths.explain: 2023 − 1853 = 170. Count up: from 1853 to 1953 is 100 years, and from 1953 to 2023 is 70 more. 100 + 70 = 170.
maths.context: This is about the Time-line Rope, where you put transport inventions in order.
maths.why_maths: Working out the gap between dates shows how fast transport has changed.

maths.problem: In the Words Only test, a silent round took 2 minutes and scored 3 out of 8. A round with questions took 5 minutes and scored 7 out of 8. How many more points did the round with questions score? How many more minutes did it take?
maths.explain: 7 − 3 = 4 more points. 5 − 2 = 3 more minutes. So questions gave a much better drawing, but took longer. Whether it is worth it depends on the job.
maths.context: This is about the Words Only test, where one person describes a picture and the other draws it without seeing it.
maths.why_maths: Comparing both the gain and the cost helps us choose: a quick message or a correct one.

roots.context: We have learned how people, goods and messages travel. In the Seen in the Dark test, we found that a driver sees us only by the light that bounces off us. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Seen in the Dark test, the same dim torch shone on every cloth. The black cloth vanished a few steps away. The white cloth was seen from much further. Both were there the whole time. A driver knows you are on the road only when light from you reaches their eyes.
deep_truth.habit: We think that being somewhere is the same as being seen there, and that if we can see a car, its driver can see us. The Seen in the Dark test showed that being seen depends on how much light comes back from us. Road safety needs both: we must see, and we must be seen.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Seen in the Dark test, every cloth stayed on the chair and got the same torch light. Only the light reflected back to the eye changed, and the black cloth vanished first. A reflective strip, which sends light straight back to the lamp, shone brightest of all.

three.who_am_i: Other people see you only because light bounces off you and goes into their eyes. When your friend looks at your face, that light is what has travelled from you to them.
three.what_is_life: Bees dance, ants leave smell trails, crows call and plants release smells that warn their neighbours. Living beings are always sending messages.
three.what_is_this_world: Roads, rails, wires and radio waves join far places, so rice from Andhra Pradesh reaches a kitchen in Kochi.

roots.thread: Every message needs a sender, something that carries it, and a receiver. In the Seen in the Dark test, the torch, the cloth and your eye made one chain. If any part was missing, nothing was seen. Roads, rails, wires and radio waves are longer chains of the same kind.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: The Charvakas taught that perception, what our senses show us, is the only sure way to know anything. In the Seen in the Dark test, there came a point where you could not see the black cloth. Yet you said it was still there, because you remembered putting it on the chair. A Charvaka would ask: can you really know something that your senses cannot show you right now?

practice.say: Let's sit still in a dim room with only one small light on. Look slowly around. Name one thing you can see. Now find where its light comes from. Open them again and notice the light coming back to you.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the listed materials. The Seen in the Dark test depends on two things: a dark background behind the cloth, and a dim enough torch. With a bare phone torch, even a black cloth may stay visible across a small room, so the torch is covered with a hanky folded into 4 layers, and the step says to add layers if needed. If a white wall is behind the chair, the black cloth shows up as a dark shape, so the chair stands in a doorway with a dark room behind it, or in front of a dark bedsheet. The child steps back heel to toe, which gives about 15 to 25 foot-steps in most flat rooms. A grown-up walks beside them and the floor is cleared first. The reflective strip step is optional, because not every home has one. The Words Only test needs only two people, paper and a clock, and the two pairs of rounds are balanced so practice does not favour one kind of round. Sign Snap has 19 cards and works for one child alone. Send It! has 12 job cards and 15 means cards, and a job without a matching card cannot come up. The spine (intro, Kitchen Journey, Seen in the Dark, explanations, roots and quiz) fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: By the 1890s, scientists knew that radio waves travel in straight lines, like light. The Earth is round, so a straight line soon leaves the ground and heads off into space. Most experts therefore thought radio could never reach much beyond the horizon, perhaps a few hundred kilometres. Guglielmo Marconi, a young Italian inventor, tried anyway. In December 1901 he set up a receiver on a hill in Newfoundland, with its wire held up by a kite. He reported hearing three faint clicks, the letter S in Morse code, sent from Cornwall in England, about 3,400 kilometres away across the Atlantic. Some people doubted he really heard it. But within a few years his stations were sending messages across the ocean every day. In 1902, Arthur Kennelly and Oliver Heaviside suggested a reason: a layer of charged air high above the Earth that bends radio waves back down. In 1924, Edward Appleton and Miles Barnett proved it. They sent radio waves up from a BBC transmitter and timed the echoes coming back from this layer. Today we call it the ionosphere.
how_we_found_out.who: Guglielmo Marconi, Arthur Kennelly, Oliver Heaviside, Edward Appleton and Miles Barnett
how_we_found_out.when: 1901 (the signal across the Atlantic), 1902 (the idea of a reflecting layer), 1924 (Appleton and Barnett's proof)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Experts thought that because radio waves travel in straight lines, they could never follow the curve of the Earth to faraway places. Marconi's signal across the Atlantic showed that radio could go much further. The reason was a charged layer high in the air, the ionosphere, which sends some radio waves back down to the ground.
how_we_found_out.context: How can a radio message travel all the way across the sea, when the Earth is round? This card tells the true story of the first signal sent across the Atlantic and of what scientists found out afterwards.

quiz: People used boats long before they used wheels.
Log canoes about 10,000 years old have been found. The oldest wheels are about 5,500 years old.
If I can see a car, the driver can see me.
You see the bright lamp itself. The driver sees you only by the little light that bounces off you.
At night, a driver sees pale clothes from further away than dark clothes.
Pale colours reflect much more headlight back to the driver than dark colours do.
Electric scooters cause no pollution at all.
The electricity may come from burning coal, and making batteries and tyres also harms the air and land.
In two-way communication, the listener can ask questions.
Both sides can send and receive, so mistakes get cleared up.
One-way communication always gets a message across more correctly than two-way.
Two-way usually works better, because the listener can ask. It only takes a little longer.
On Indian road signs, a circle gives an order and a triangle gives a warning.
Shape and colour carry the message, so signs can be read from far away without words.
Bright neon colours keep you easy to see at night.
Neon colours glow with invisible light from the Sun. Headlights give out almost none of it, so neon colours do not glow at night.
Some radio waves bounce off a layer of charged air and reach beyond the horizon.
This layer, the ionosphere, bends them back to the ground far away.
Petrol and diesel exhaust only warms the Earth and does not hurt our lungs.
Exhaust also has soot and harmful gases that hurt the lungs, as well as carbon dioxide that warms the Earth.
odd: The first three are two-way, so both sides can answer. A TV show sends a message one way to many people.
The first three send much light back to the driver at night. A black shirt sends back very little.
The first three carry a liquid or gas through a long pipe. A truck carries goods along a road.
The first three are ways living beings send a message to others. A falling leaf carries no message.
The first three send messages using electricity. A drum sends sound without electricity.
